::: {#brief .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-cap-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The brief</p>
<p class="lx-case-q">Prairieland's energy minister wants a pathway to 2050 for its five regions, and its defense: cost, CO₂ against the budget, security, who pays and Ridge County's jobs.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Also: how the pathway holds up against a gas-price spike, a drought, a mineral export restriction and a demand surprise.</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Hand in:</b> a pathway link; a policy brief, two pages of your own writing with the evidence your run adds (the shock table is its sensitivity); and the lines M13's notebook prints for the same pathway.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> the <a href="sb4-pathway-explorer.html">Pathway Explorer</a>'s engine, its costs and fuels within their fixed ranges, and lesson <a href="a13-fairness-jobs.html">A13</a>'s accounting layer for who pays and for jobs (Prairieland is fictional; its numbers are illustrative).</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> every check under the brief is in place, and the self-check reaches Proficient on every competence.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 240 minutes: 70 to build and test pathways, 30 to read the results, 40 to run your pathway in <a href="m13-national-pathway.html">M13</a>'s notebook, 70 to write the brief, 30 to check it.</p>
<dl class="lx-sb-facts c4-units">
<div><dt>Units</dt><dd>Power in GW; energy in TWh and PJ (1 TWh = 3.6 PJ; 1 PJ = a million GJ); CO₂ in Mt, million tonnes; fuel prices per GJ on <span class="lx-term" data-term="net-calorific-value">net calorific values</span>.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Terms</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="primary-energy">Primary energy</span>: fuels as found, before conversion. <span class="lx-term" data-term="lng">LNG</span>: liquefied natural gas. The LP's dual: the modeled cost change from tightening the budget by one tonne.</dd></div>
<div><dt>More terms</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="linear-program">LP</span>: linear program. <span class="lx-term" data-term="firm-capacity">Firm clean</span>: the generic plant that runs steadily, within its availability. <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-burden">Energy burden</span>: home-energy spending ÷ household income.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Cost terms</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="present-value">Present value</span>: future costs in today's dollars, discounted. <span class="lx-term" data-term="fixed-om">Fixed O&amp;M</span>: a plant's yearly upkeep. <span class="lx-term" data-term="net-demand">Net load</span>: demand less wind and solar. <span class="lx-term" data-term="round-trip-efficiency">85% round trip</span>: a battery returns 85% of what it takes in.</dd></div>
</dl>
</div>
```

2035 runs what was built; later years re-plan.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-eyebrow">The default pathway's assumptions, for the brief</p><ul class="c4-assume"><li>Prairieland and Ridge County are fictional; their numbers are illustrative.</li><li>2025 dollars; costs are fixed ranges the plan sets, the same in every period, whatever is built.</li><li>The cost counts the existing wind, solar and batteries' fixed O&amp;M while they are open.</li><li>The data give no fixed O&amp;M for existing hydro and the steady plants, so their upkeep is left out (the same in every pathway).</li><li>An existing plant leaves the plan in the five-year period that contains its retirement year: a conservative simplification.</li><li>Twelve time slices of 2025's weather stand for each model year; the peak net-load day and the scarce-wind week get their own average day and night, not their hourly sequence.</li><li>A peak-hour rule at two stress hours of 2025, each region's load plus 10%.</li><li>CO₂: fuels burned inside Prairieland at the IPCC's factors; the budget counts 2025 twice and the model years with straight lines between (weights 2, 5, 5, 5, 5, 3).</li><li>Electrification follows the plan; end-use equipment (heat pumps, cars, boilers) is left out of every cost.</li><li>Operating shocks (the gas-price spike, the drought, the demand surprise) keep the plan's builds through their year, which runs what was built; later years re-plan.</li><li>The mineral restriction raises a purchase price: decisions through the year before it are kept, and its year's batteries are bought again at its price.</li><li>Affordability: households pay 50% of the change in 2050's yearly cost against the 2025-policies pathway, per kWh; Prairie City's five groups stand in for Prairieland's households.</li><li>That 2050 difference is laid on 2025's households: their income, spending and electricity use stay at 2025's, so the burden is a screening comparison, not a forecast for 2050.</li><li>The households' share (50%) is spread in full over the household groups; the rest of the change is outside this screening.</li><li>Each group is its average household; households within a group differ.</li><li>Use does not change when the price changes (no response to the charge).</li><li>Ridge County: mine jobs scale with coal mined at A13's ratio (5.22 jobs per PJ).</li><li>New jobs come from all the wind and solar built in the Ridge region, assumed to be in Ridge County: an upper bound for the county.</li><li>Jobs use A13's coefficients, a multiplier of 1.6 and 20% displacement.</li><li>Lost jobs count in full: no re-employment of the plant's or mines' workers is assumed.</li><li>The multiplier turns direct (on-site) jobs into direct, supplier and spending jobs, the same on both sides.</li><li>Displacement, new work that would have existed anyway, comes off every count marked net; gross counts keep it.</li><li>Full-year check (2030 and 2050, two weathers): 4 of 4 pass, all demand served and CO₂ within 10% of the slices (a teaching tolerance); it does not test the budget.</li></ul>

<div class="lx-datanote c4-note"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><ul>
<li><b>Illustrative:</b> Prairieland, its regions, fleet, links, demand, shocks and Ridge County (prairieland.json); the existing plants' operating costs, the penalties and the peak-hour rule (e4-pathways.json); A13's jobs coefficients.</li>
<li><b>Based on public data:</b> new plants' costs from EIA's 2026 assumptions, fuel prices from EIA's 2025 data, CO₂ factors from the IPCC, hourly shapes from SPP's 2025 and 2024 grid.</li>
<li><b>Left out of every cost:</b> end-use equipment (heat pumps, cars, boilers), so a pathway that electrifies more looks cheaper than it would be for households.</li>
<li><b>Also left out:</b> the upkeep of the existing hydro and steady plants (the data give no figure; the same in every pathway).</li>
<li><b>Who pays and jobs:</b> <a href="a13-fairness-jobs.html">A13</a>'s accounting layer: screening estimates with stated assumptions, not outputs of the linear program; Prairie City's five household groups stand in for Prairieland's.</li>
<li><b>Precomputed:</b> the first view and the presets' full-year checks (about a minute of solving each) come from a library made with this engine; every run you start solves in your browser.</li>
<li><b>Against lesson A20:</b> no pathway here gets below about 2,700 Mt (straight-line counting, central demand). <a href="a20-national-scenarios.html">A20</a> meets 2,600 Mt because its fastest path electrifies buildings and industry years sooner.</li>
<li><details class="e4-corr"><summary><b>Corrected 8 Nov 2026:</b></summary> <span>the import cap's base now leaves out what batteries and links lose, so electricity lost there no longer helps meet it. Security first: $438.2 billion, was $520.4 billion.</span> <span>A run that misses a limit shows no electricity prices; the scarce-wind week's battery energy is paid back on winter days.</span></details></li>
<li><details class="e4-corr"><summary><b>Corrected 7 Nov 2026:</b></summary> <span>costs now include the existing wind, solar and batteries' fixed O&amp;M, the same in every pathway at one discount rate ($9.1 billion at 5%; central: $410.7 billion, was $401.6 billion). The full-year check buys gas in the slice run's own mix.</span></details></li>
</ul></div>

::: {#note .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Write your two-page policy brief
:::

```{=html}
<div id="c4-note" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- c4-note:start -->
<ol class="lx-rn-outline"><li><b>Title and plan link:</b> the plan's link from the bench, and the date</li><li><b>Recommendation:</b> Three or four sentences: the pathway Prairieland should take to 2050, and why.</li><li><b>The plan:</b> each choice, with its unit</li><li><b>Results:</b> each result, with its unit and boundary</li><li><b>Assumptions:</b> one sentence each</li><li><b>Sensitivity:</b> how one result moves when one input changes, and whether the plan was held fixed</li><li><b>Cost, carbon and security:</b> Two or three sentences: the cost, CO₂ against the budget, imports against the cap.</li><li><b>Shocks and what would change the recommendation:</b> Two or three sentences: what the four shocks did, and which result would make you choose differently.</li><li><b>Who pays, and Ridge County:</b> Two or three sentences: households (a screening estimate, with your share and design) and Ridge County's jobs, gross and net.</li><li><b>M13's notebook on your pathway:</b> Paste the lines its section 8 printed for your plan (cost, CO₂, imports, what it builds) and say whether they match the page.</li><li><b>Sources and credit:</b> One or two sentences: the data behind your numbers (EIA, IPCC, SPP through EIA-930; the course's teaching settings) and any conflict of interest.</li><li><b>Limits of this analysis:</b> what the model leaves out</li></ol>
<!-- c4-note:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-notebook c4-nb" id="c4-nb">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Part of the hand-in · your pathway in M13's notebook, about 40 minutes</p>
<ol class="c4-nb-steps">
<li>Open <a href="m13-national-pathway.html">M13</a>'s notebook with its three data files, as you did in M13.</li>
<li>In its section 8, set <code>MY = </code> to your pathway's levers (the Pathway Explorer's keys).</li>
<li>Run it. It solves the same linear program and prints the cost, CO₂ by model year, imports, what it builds and a link to the same plan.</li>
<li>Paste those lines into the brief's notebook field, and say whether they match the page.</li>
</ol>
</div>
```
:::

:::

<b>Why this one:</b> a security-first plan (imports at most 25%) costs $27.4 billion more and still cannot meet its cap in 2030 [2].

<b>Shocks:</b> Cost: against the four shocks, each re-planned from its year, the cost to 2050 moves by $0.0 billion to +$26.5 billion, most for the demand surprise [5].
<b>Under the shocks:</b> Carbon: the budget is met under all four. Imports: within the cap under all four. Peak hours: short of the rule in the shock's year under the drought and the demand surprise [6].
<b>What would change it:</b> the demand surprise costs most (+$26.5 billion) and leaves the stress hours 4,766 MW short in 2035; if it looked likely, I would build more firm capacity before 2035 [7].
<b>Who pays (screening):</b> about $−130 a household a year in 2050 if households pay 50%; equipment not counted [8].
<b>Ridge County (screening):</b> 5,533 jobs lost against 1,152 new ongoing jobs (922 net), with a multiplier of 1.6, 20% displacement and all the Ridge region's new wind and solar in the county [9].
<b>Evidence:</b> the plan link, c4-prairieland-2050.html#c4-v1-d1-eb80-et50-ei55-b3600-a0-c40-f0-m2-fm1-t1-r1-cw1712-cs1484-cb1521-cc1032-ct1158-cf7000-cx1500-pg4d05-pl10-pc2d41-po12-dr5-hs50-rc0-jm1d6-jd20; M13's notebook on the same plan prints “cost to 2050 $410.7 billion (present value); CO2 2026-2050 3,600 Mt”, the page's numbers [10].

</div>
